```{r}
#| label: setup-biomarkers
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(randomForest)

trim_fn <- function(x){
  x[x > 3] <- 3
  x[x < -3] <- -3
  return(x)
}

# Retain the supplied preprocessing for this descriptive demonstration.
# For predictive evaluation, estimate preprocessing using training data only.
asd_clean <- read_csv('data/biomarker-clean.csv') %>%
  select(-ados) %>%
  mutate(across(.cols = -group, log10)) %>%
  mutate(across(.cols = -group, ~ scale(.x)[, 1])) %>%
  mutate(across(.cols = -group, trim_fn))

asd_preds <- asd_clean %>% select(-group)
asd_resp <- asd_clean %>% pull(group) %>% factor()
```

## Random forests: recap

Last time, we combined predictions from trees using a majority vote.

-   Each tree uses a bootstrap sample of observations

-   At each split, consider a random subset of predictors

-   Combine predictions across many trees

. . .

For the biomarker analysis, we also use the forest to ***rank proteins by variable importance.***

## Which proteins appear important?

Gini importance summarizes the reduction in node impurity attributed to each predictor across the forest.

```{r}
#| label: fit-random-forest
set.seed(102025)
rf_out <- randomForest(x = asd_preds,
                       y = asd_resp,
                       ntree = 1000,
                       importance = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: plot-importance
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-align: center
rf_out$importance %>%
  as_tibble(rownames = 'protein') %>%
  slice_max(MeanDecreaseGini, n = 10, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
  ggplot(aes(y = reorder(protein, MeanDecreaseGini),
             x = MeanDecreaseGini)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = 'Mean decrease in Gini index', y = 'Protein')
```

::: notes
Spend about two minutes here. An importance score describes the fitted model.
It does not establish a biological mechanism or provide a significance test.
Correlated predictors can complicate interpretation of individual rankings.
:::

## Selecting a core panel

For this example, compare the top 10 proteins from:

-   multiple testing, ranked by adjusted p-value

-   random forest variable importance

$$
\hat{S}^* = \hat{S}_{\text{testing}} \cap \hat{S}_{\text{forest}}
$$

```{r}
#| label: select-panel
tt_fn <- function(.df){
  infer::t_test(.df,
               formula = level ~ group,
               alternative = 'two-sided',
               order = c('ASD', 'TD'),
               var.equal = FALSE)
}

test_results <- asd_clean %>%
  pivot_longer(-group, names_to = 'protein', values_to = 'level') %>%
  nest(data = c(group, level)) %>%
  mutate(test = map(data, tt_fn)) %>%
  unnest(test) %>%
  mutate(p.adj = p.adjust(p_value, method = 'BY'))

s1 <- test_results %>%
  arrange(p.adj, p_value, protein) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)

s2 <- rf_out$importance %>%
  as_tibble(rownames = 'protein') %>%
  arrange(desc(MeanDecreaseGini), protein) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)

s_star <- intersect(s1, s2)
if (length(s_star) == 0L) {
  stop('The two top-10 lists have no overlap. Review the panel selection before rendering.')
}
knitr::kable(tibble(Protein = s_star))
```

::: notes
The supplied code intersects two lists, so the text now consistently says
two methods. Selecting the top 10 is a ranking rule, not a significance cutoff.
The BY adjustment now uses p.adjust rather than a hand-computed approximation.
:::

## Logistic regression: recap

Let $Y_i = 1$ indicate ASD and $Y_i = 0$ indicate TD.

$$
\log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip}
$$

-   Predictors: proteins in the selected panel

-   Output: estimated probability of ASD

-   Classification rule for this example: predict ASD when $\hat{p}_i > 0.5$

## Fitting the panel model

```{r}
#| label: fit-panel
#| echo: true
asd_sub <- asd_clean %>%
  select(group, all_of(s_star)) %>%
  mutate(group = (group == 'ASD'))

fit <- glm(group ~ ., family = 'binomial', data = asd_sub)
```

. . .

The modeling function is the same whether we include one protein or several.

::: notes
Use this as a short code walkthrough rather than a live coding exercise.
The panel selection and model fit do not depend on anything in the guest block.
:::

## Measuring classification accuracy

```{r}
#| label: panel-predictions
pred_df <- asd_sub %>%
  modelr::add_predictions(fit, type = 'response') %>%
  transmute(
    group = factor(group, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c('TD', 'ASD')),
    pred,
    pred_class = factor(pred > 0.5,
                        levels = c(FALSE, TRUE), labels = c('TD', 'ASD'))
  )

table(Actual = pred_df$group, Predicted = pred_df$pred_class) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

-   **Sensitivity:** proportion of ASD observations classified as ASD

-   **Specificity:** proportion of TD observations classified as TD

-   **Accuracy:** proportion of all observations classified correctly

## What do these results tell us?

```{r}
#| label: panel-metrics
class_metrics <- yardstick::metric_set(
  yardstick::sensitivity, yardstick::specificity, yardstick::accuracy
)

class_metrics(pred_df, truth = group, estimate = pred_class,
              event_level = 'second') %>%
  select(.metric, .estimate) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

***These are training results.*** We used these observations to select proteins, fit the model, and calculate accuracy.

. . .

To evaluate predictions for new subjects, repeat preprocessing and protein selection within the training portion of each split, then evaluate on held-out observations.

::: notes
Ask briefly why holding out data only after selecting the proteins would still
leak information. Save an extended design discussion for Thursday.
:::

<!-- ## Random forest settings -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| echo: true -->
<!-- #| eval: false -->
<!-- rf_out <- randomForest(x = asd_preds, -->
<!--                        y = asd_resp, -->
<!--                        ntree = 1000, -->
<!--                        importance = TRUE) -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- Settings include the number of trees, predictors considered ***at each split***, bootstrap sample size, and node size. -->

<!-- For classification, the default `mtry` is $\lfloor\sqrt{p}\rfloor$. -->

<!-- The default bootstrap sample has $n$ draws with replacement. Default classification trees grow to purity where possible, subject to the data and stopping rules. -->

<!-- ## Measuring split quality -->

<!-- If $p_k$ is the proportion of observations in class $k$, two measures of node impurity are: -->

<!-- -   Gini index: $1 - \sum_{k=1}^K p_k^2$ -->

<!-- -   Entropy: $-\sum_{k=1}^K p_k\log_2 p_k$ -->

<!-- . . . -->

<!-- Smaller values indicate greater homogeneity. -->

<!-- For child-node proportions $w_L$ and $w_R$, the reduction in impurity is -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- h(\text{parent}) - \left[w_L h(\text{left}) + w_R h(\text{right})\right]. -->
<!-- $$ -->

<!-- ## Interpreting importance -->

<!-- Counting how often a variable appears in a tree ignores the quality of its splits. -->

<!-- Gini importance accumulates weighted decreases in Gini impurity attributed to a predictor and averages across trees. -->

<!-- -   Larger values indicate a greater contribution to reducing impurity -->

<!-- -   Correlated predictors can share or compete for importance -->

<!-- -   Importance does not establish causation or statistical significance -->

<!-- ``` -->

<!-- The confusion matrix returned by `randomForest()` uses ***out-of-bag*** predictions. -->

<!-- Each observation receives votes from trees whose bootstrap samples excluded it. -->

<!-- . . . -->

<!-- ## The Bernoulli distribution -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- Y \sim \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p) -->
<!-- \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad -->
<!-- P(Y=y)=p^y(1-p)^{1-y},\qquad y\in\{0,1\}. -->
<!-- $$ -->

<!-- This gives $P(Y=1)=p$ and $P(Y=0)=1-p$. -->

<!-- -   $\mathbb{E}(Y)=p$ -->

<!-- -   $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=p(1-p)$ -->

<!-- ## Logistic regression model and interpretation -->

<!-- For conditionally independent observations, -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- Y_i\mid X_i=x_i\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(p_i), -->
<!-- \qquad -->
<!-- \log\left(\frac{p_i}{1-p_i}\right)=\beta_0+\sum_{j=1}^p\beta_jx_{ij}. -->
<!-- $$ -->

<!-- For an additive model, a one-unit increase in $x_j$, holding other predictors fixed, changes: -->

<!-- -   log-odds by $\beta_j$ -->

<!-- -   odds by a factor of $e^{\beta_j}$ -->

<!-- The assumed linear relationship is on the ***log-odds scale***. -->

<!-- ## The model, visually -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- p_i=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x_i^T\beta}} -->
<!-- $$ -->

<!-- ```{r} -->
<!-- #| fig-width: 6 -->
<!-- #| fig-height: 3 -->
<!-- #| fig-align: center -->
<!-- fx <- function(x, a, b){ -->
<!--   1/(1 + exp(-(a + x*b))) -->
<!-- } -->
<!-- curve(fx(x, 0, 1), from = -10, to = 10, -->
<!--       xlab = 'x', ylab = 'P(Y = 1)') -->
<!-- ``` -->

<!-- ## Maximum likelihood -->

<!-- Maximum likelihood selects parameters that maximize the likelihood of the observed outcomes given the predictors. -->

<!-- Equivalently, minimize the negative log-likelihood: -->

<!-- $$ -->
<!-- \hat{\beta}=\arg\min_\beta\{-\ell(\beta;x,y)\}. -->
<!-- $$ -->

<!-- `glm()` fits the model using iteratively reweighted least squares. -->

<!-- ## Accuracy calculations -->

<!-- |          | Predicted TD        | Predicted ASD       | -->
<!-- |----------|---------------------|---------------------| -->
<!-- | True TD  | True negative (TN)  | False positive (FP) | -->
<!-- | True ASD | False negative (FN) | True positive (TP)  | -->

<!-- -   Sensitivity: $TP/(TP+FN)$ -->

<!-- -   Specificity: $TN/(TN+FP)$ -->

<!-- -   Accuracy: $(TP+TN)/(TP+TN+FP+FN)$ -->

<!-- ## Other accuracy metrics -->

<!-- -   Precision: $TP/(TP+FP)$, the proportion of predicted positives that are positive -->

<!-- -   False discovery proportion: $FP/(TP+FP)$ for the observed classifications -->

<!-- -   F1 score: $2TP/(2TP+FP+FN)$, the harmonic mean of precision and recall -->

<!-- -   AUROC: area under the ROC curve -->

<!-- The choice of metric should reflect the consequences of different errors. -->
